summary: Zstandard can use different window sizes, which limit memory use during compression and decompression. Some browsers cap the window size, which causes interoperability trouble. This document turns the recommended limit from RFC 8878 into a requirement for HTTP content encoding.

eli5.summary: Squishing a file needs a memory workspace of some size. If the sender uses a bigger one than the receiver can handle, things break. This sets a size limit so both sides can cope.

subtitle: A hard 8 MB window limit so zstd-compressed web content decodes everywhere.

tldr.problem: Zstandard encoders can pick very large window sizes, but some browsers and user agents refuse to decode content above a limit they set to protect memory. The result is failed responses.
tldr.mechanism: For the "zstd" HTTP content coding, decoders MUST support a Window_Size of up to and including 8 MB, and encoders MUST NOT generate frames that need more than 8 MB.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8878 only recommended the 8 MB figure; this document makes it a requirement in HTTP contexts, and it updates the "zstd" entry in the IANA registry to match.

today: RFC 9659 is an Informational document that updates RFC 8878. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Window Size Problem
sections.content:
Zstandard ("zstd"), specified in RFC 8878, is a lossless compression mechanism similar to gzip. In HTTP, the zstd content coding token tells the decoder that the content is Zstandard-compressed.

Compressed data carries a Window_Size: the maximum distance for back-references, and so how much of the content must stay in memory while decompressing. The minimum is 1 KB and the maximum is (1<<41) + 7*(1<<38) bytes, which is 3.75 TB. Bigger windows tend to compress better but use more memory.

To protect against unreasonable memory use, some browsers and user agents limit the Window_Size they will handle. Content compressed with a larger window then fails to decode, which hurts interoperability.
sections.eli5: A bigger workspace squishes files smaller but needs more room. Some programs only have a small desk, so they cannot open files that were squished on a giant one.

sections.title: The 8 MB Requirement
sections.content:
RFC 8878, Section 3.1.1.1.2, recommends that decoders support a Window_Size of up to 8 MB and that encoders not generate frames with a larger one, but it imposes no requirements. This document turns that into a rule for the zstd HTTP content coding.

Decoders MUST support a Window_Size of up to and including 8 MB. Encoders MUST NOT generate frames requiring a Window_Size larger than 8 MB. With both sides bound, a sender can rely on any receiver being able to decode its output.
sections.eli5: Everyone agrees on one desk size: 8 MB. Senders must not use a bigger one, and receivers must be able to handle at least that much.

sections.title: Security and Registry Notes
sections.content:
The document introduces no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 8878. It does warn that decoders still need to expect oversized frames that break the limit, and must fail decoding when they receive such invalid frames.

On the IANA side, the entry for zstd in the HTTP Content Coding Registry is updated. Its description becomes a stream of bytes compressed using the Zstandard protocol with a Window_Size of not more than 8 MB, and its reference is this document and RFC 8878.
sections.eli5: A careful receiver still checks the size, and refuses any file that breaks the rule. The official list of names is updated to say the limit too.
